rgb: The camera wearer is seated and looking down at a tiled floor, with a white towel draped across their lap 0.2 to 0.4 metres below the camera and a low white-and-cyan rectangular platform featuring a black oval cutout positioned directly ahead at 0.5 to 0.7 metres. A second person is seated opposite on a cyan seat approximately 0.6 to 1.0 metres away and faces the camera wearer, although only their lower legs in dark trousers and their bare feet fitted with white toe separators appear near the frame’s top; their head and upper body extend beyond the upper edge. Their feet are set roughly 0.3 to 0.4 metres apart, flanking the black cutout, and a rack containing upright bottles stands on the floor to the platform’s right, around 0.8 to 1.0 metres from the wearer and 0.2 metres from the platform. In frame 1, the wearer grips a plastic-lined blue oval basin with both hands directly over the platform at about 0.5 metres, blocking its right side and the other person’s left foot. They then rotate to the right through frames 2 and 3 and set the basin on the floor right of the platform, about 0.6 to 0.8 metres away. During frames 4 and 5, the wearer turns back toward the center-left, revealing on the far left a white side table 0.3 to 0.5 metres away that supports a blue basket, a yellow bottle, and hand tools. They raise the white towel with both hands to 0.3 to 0.4 metres in front of the camera, where it partly hides the platform and floor basin. The towel, blue basin, platform, other person’s feet, and left-side tool table remain within the wearer’s arm’s reach throughout, all under 0.8 metres away.
depth: The monocular depth image presents a downward-looking view in which the seated camera wearer faces a second seated person while viewing their own arms, hands, and lap, shown brightest at 0.3–0.6 m away. Opposite, the second person’s lower legs and bare feet with toe separators sit on an elevated pedicure footrest box, rendered mid-grey at 0.7–1.0 m and positioned about 0.3–0.5 m beyond the wearer’s hands, over a dark tiled floor lying 1.1–1.4 m below the camera. From frames 1 through 3, the wearer raises an oval blue basin from above the footrest at roughly 0.6 m; in frame 1 it partly blocks the footrest and the other person’s right foot. The basin is then placed on the floor to the right, becoming darker grey as it recedes to 1.1–1.3 m in frames 3–4. In frames 4–5, the wearer brings a white towel up from their lap toward the camera to 0.4–0.5 m, as a tall supply cart appears at the far left at 0.5–0.7 m. The footrest, basin, towel, cart, and other person’s feet all stay within the camera wearer’s arm’s reach. Because the other person’s head and upper body are entirely outside the top edge, their gaze toward the wearer cannot be observed directly, although their feet point toward the wearer. Relative to RGB alone, the depth map clearly distinguishes the elevated vertical positions of the footrest and left-side supply cart from the lower floor, while tracing the basin’s descent from lap height to floor level. Its estimates are nevertheless unreliable in frame 3, where the other person’s upper-left legs and the footrest box are excessively bright and seem nearer than the wearer’s hands, and in frame 4, where the footrest’s black cushion appears as a smooth convex mound instead of a flat surface.
segmentation: The instance-segmentation view separates foreground areas within the pedicure workspace: the camera wearer’s outstretched arms at the bottom, 0.3–0.6 m from the camera; the oval basin across the central-to-right area, descending from 0.6 m to 1.2 m on the floor during frames 1–3; and the second person’s lower legs and feet at the top-left, 0.7–1.0 m away and oriented toward the wearer while their upper body remains outside the frame. Through frames 1 to 3, the basin’s mask travels rightward and becomes smaller as the basin is lowered from above the footrest onto the floor at the right, clearing its previous occlusion of the footrest. In frames 4 and 5, one large mask instead encompasses the wearer’s arms, lap towel, and the other person’s feet across the center and bottom. The basin, towel, and other person’s feet are each within the camera wearer’s arm’s reach, no farther than 0.8 m, with separations of 0.2–0.5 m between them. Although the masks clearly outline the oval basin’s crisp silhouette and rightward movement, along with the foreground limbs against the unsegmented floor, both their semantic labels and instance boundaries are highly unreliable. The system labels the blue pedicure basin as a ‘frisbee’ in frames 1–2 and as a ‘person’ in frame 3; divides the wearer’s two arms and the other person’s legs into separate ‘person’ instances in frames 2–3; combines the wearer’s arms, white towel, footrest cushion, and the other person’s feet into one ‘person’ mask in frames 4–5; and entirely fails to detect the footrest box, nail polish rack, and left-side tool cart.
pose: The pose visualization overlays yellow 2D body skeletons and magenta hand landmarks within the camera wearer’s nearby workspace, 0.3–0.8 m away. It records both the wearer’s left and right hands holding the basin rims in frames 1 and 2 while the basin travels rightward, only the right hand gripping the rim in frame 3, and both hands raised nearer the camera at 0.4–0.5 m while holding the white towel in frames 4 and 5. In frames 4–5, the map tracks the hands drawing inward, changing from roughly 0.4 m apart while holding the basin to about 0.15 m apart as they bunch the towel. It also depicts the elbows bending outward along either side of the lap, within arm’s reach of the other person’s feet positioned immediately above at 0.7–1.0 m away. The display makes the wearer’s subtle finger bending and grip direction visible even where the basin rim or folds of the white towel partly obscure the hands in RGB. However, it is seriously unreliable for global spatial arrangement and interpretation of multiple people: it entirely omits the wearer’s left hand in frame 3 and fails to detect the second person’s legs and feet in frames 2–5. In addition, the top-down egocentric perspective cuts off both individuals’ heads and torsos, causing the estimator to invent miniature, upside-down complete torso-and-head skeletons over the other person’s feet and the footrest in frame 1, and over the camera wearer’s lap towel and arms in frames 4 and 5, thereby producing incorrect body-orientation signals.
